clue.text: Part politics at Willy Russell's convenience

definitions.text: Part politics at Willy Russell's convenience

parts.words: Part politics at Willy Russell's convenience
parts.note: the title of Willy Russell's play set in a public lavatory (a 'convenience'), and the names of two kinds of pre-wedding party, one for men and one for women

explanation.walkthrough: 'Part politics' plays on 'party politics': the two sexes hold separate parties before a wedding. Willy Russell's play of that name is set in the gents' and ladies' of a Liverpool dance hall, a British 'convenience'.
explanation.definitionFit: Willy Russell's 1978 comedy carries this title, which also names the separate bachelor and bachelorette parties.

clue.text: Shakespearean bit-part player in auction on river

parts.note: a sale by auction, so auction gives sale
rio is Spanish and Portuguese for river

explanation.surface: An actor with a tiny Shakespearean role is put up for sale beside a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Salerio is a minor Venetian gentleman, a friend of Antonio, in The Merchant of Venice.

clue.text: Hartley predator

parts.note: L. P. Hartley's novel pairs a shrimp with a sea creature that preys on it, as the boy and girl of the story are paired

explanation.walkthrough: L. P. Hartley's novel The Shrimp and the — names its predator in the title; the clue relies on knowing that book.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hartley's title the tentacled sea creature is the shrimp's predator, mirroring the dominant sister Hilda.

clue.text: Dickensian swinger who married Sophorina Sphynx

definitions.text: Dickensian swinger who married Sophorina Sphynx

parts.words: Dickensian swinger who married Sophorina Sphynx
parts.note: Dick of The Old Curiosity Shop, whose surname suggests something that swings on a pivot, married the servant girl he renamed Sophronia Sphynx

explanation.surface: A Dickens rake weds a woman with an exotic name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swinger' suggests a rake, but it points to the surname: a swivel turns or swings. Dick married the Marchioness, whom he renamed Sophronia Sphynx.
explanation.definitionFit: Dick in The Old Curiosity Shop marries the Brasses' downtrodden maid, the Marchioness, after renaming her Sophronia Sphynx.

clue.text: "Down the -n rocks… he pours his urn" (James Thompson)

definitions.text: "Down the -n rocks… he pours his urn" (James Thompson)

parts.words: "Down the -n rocks… he pours his urn" (James Thompson)
parts.note: a gap-fill: James Thomson's Seasons has the Nile pour its urn down rocks named after an African region, and the printed -n is added to the missing word

explanation.surface: A line of eighteenth-century verse about a river god pouring his urn down rocks.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap plus the printed -n makes the adjective in Thomson's line about the Nile, so the answer is the region the rocks belong to. The setter spells the poet Thompson; he is James Thomson of The Seasons.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nile flows north through this ancient region of Sudan and southern Egypt, whose cataracts are the rocks of the line.

clue.text: One with leisure pursuit loses unknown quantity as supporter of political philosopher

indicators.note: loses says a letter is taken away from the word before it

parts.note: someone with a pastime is a hobbyist
x, y and z stand for unknowns in algebra; here y

explanation.surface: A man with a hobby gives up something mysterious and becomes a follower of a philosopher.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking the Y from HOBBYIST leaves a follower of Thomas Hobbes, author of Leviathan.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower of Thomas Hobbes, the seventeenth-century English political thinker, is called by this name.

clue.text: Novelist gives direction to first-class letter writer

parts.note: N for north, a compass direction
A1 means first-class, written here as AI
Saint Paul wrote the Epistles, the letters of the New Testament

explanation.surface: A writer points the way to a top-notch correspondent.
explanation.walkthrough: A1, 'first-class', is spelt AI with the figure 1 read as the letter I. The apostle Paul is crosswords' letter writer.
explanation.definitionFit: V. S. Naipaul was a Trinidad-born Nobel-winning author of fiction such as A House for Mr Biswas.

clue.text: Man abandoned by Rose Macaulay

parts.note: the Isle of Man is an island; an island left without parents is the title of Rose Macaulay's 1924 novel

explanation.surface: A man is deserted by a woman novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' reads as a person but is the Isle of Man, a land mass; 'abandoned' turns it into a parentless one, the title of Macaulay's satire about castaways.
explanation.definitionFit: Rose Macaulay's 1924 satirical novel about shipwrecked Victorians founding a society is so titled.

clue.text: Outstanding examples of sculpture

parts.note: carvings that stand out from a background are reliefs, called by the Italian plural word

explanation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' seems to praise the work but means literally standing out from the surface: Italian reliefs.
explanation.definitionFit: These are Italian-named relief carvings, whose figures project from a flat background.

clue.text: Pompous "booster of Zenith

parts.note: Sinclair Lewis's self-satisfied businessman boosts his Midwestern home city of Zenith

explanation.walkthrough: Zenith is the fictional city of Sinclair Lewis's 1922 novel; its hero is the town's complacent booster, a word that became a byword for philistine conformity.
explanation.definitionFit: George F. Babbitt, Sinclair Lewis's estate agent, is a smug promoter of the city of Zenith.

clue.text: They are a bit of a trial for W. H. Auden

definitions.text: They are a bit of a trial for W. H. Auden

parts.words: They are a bit of a trial for W. H. Auden
parts.note: people who give evidence form a part of any court case, and Auden wrote a poem bearing that title

explanation.surface: Some people are a nuisance to the poet Auden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit of a trial' looks like 'a nuisance' but means a component of a court hearing: those who testify. Auden's poem of that name appeared in the 1930s.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who testify are part of a court trial, and Auden's poem and verse chorus bear this title.

clue.text: Lovelace seemed to love his daughter, but not honour more

definitions.text: Lovelace seemed to love his daughter, but not honour more

parts.words: Lovelace seemed to love his daughter, but not honour more
parts.note: Richardson's rake Robert Lovelace pursues Clarissa, daughter of this family, while the poet Richard Lovelace wrote 'Loved I not honour more'

explanation.surface: A suitor seems devoted to a man's daughter yet has no regard for honour.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet Richard Lovelace wrote 'I could not love thee, dear, so much, / Loved I not honour more'; Richardson's Lovelace does the opposite, dishonouring Clarissa.
explanation.definitionFit: Clarissa, or the History of a Young Lady, has a heroine of this surname, seduced and ruined by Lovelace.

clue.text: "Let onion atoms lurk within the bowl, And scarce suspected, the whole " (Revd Sydney Smith )

definitions.text: "Let onion atoms lurk within the bowl, And scarce suspected, the whole " (Revd Sydney Smith )

parts.words: "Let onion atoms lurk within the bowl, And scarce suspected, the whole " (Revd Sydney Smith )
parts.note: a gap-fill: Sydney Smith's verse recipe for salad says the hidden onion should enliven the whole dish

explanation.surface: A line from a clergyman's verse recipe for a salad.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is from Sydney Smith's 'Recipe for a Salad'; the missing verb rhymes with 'bowl' only in the eye, and means quicken or enliven.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring to life or enliven is what the trace of onion does to the salad in Smith's couplet.

clue.text: Petrified mother of twelve

parts.note: in Greek myth the queen who boasted of her many children lost them all and was turned into stone

explanation.walkthrough: 'Petrified' seems to mean terrified but means literally turned to stone. Homer gives her six sons and six daughters, killed by Apollo and Artemis.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Theban queen was turned to weeping rock after her twelve children were slain.

clue.text: Find bad backing for violinist

parts.note: to find something is to locate it

indicators.note: backing says the word for bad is written in reverse after the first piece

parts.note: ill means bad, as in ill will

explanation.surface: Track down a poor supporter for a fiddler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns ILL into LLI, which follows LOCATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Pietro Locatelli was an eighteenth-century Italian virtuoso and composer for the fiddle.

clue.text: Innocent child in one Italian composer

parts.note: a cherub is an angelic, innocent-looking child
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A guileless child lives inside an Italian musician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a container signal but is just the letters IN in the chain.
explanation.definitionFit: Luigi Cherubini was an Italian-born composer of operas such as Médée, working in Paris.

clue.text: Poet describes animals on both sides of stream

indicators.note: on both sides of says the word for animals sits around the word for stream

parts.note: swine are pigs, animals
a burn is a Scottish word for a stream

explanation.surface: A poet writes about pigs grazing either side of a brook.
explanation.walkthrough: BURN, Scots for a stream, sits inside SWINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Algernon Charles Swinburne was a Victorian writer of verse such as Poems and Ballads.

clue.text: Detached attitude of 7

parts.note: the frame of mind of an island, the subject of 7 down, cut off from others

explanation.surface: An aloof frame of mind belongs to someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The word comes from Latin insula, island, so an island's attitude is literally this: narrow and cut off.
explanation.definitionFit: Narrow-minded and cut off from outside ideas, as an island is cut off by the sea.

clue.text: Edwardian novelist and fringe dramatist

explanation.walkthrough: 'fringe' is not the Edinburgh fringe here but Beyond the Fringe, the 1960 satirical revue.
explanation.definitionFit: Arnold Bennett wrote Edwardian fiction such as The Old Wives' Tale; Alan Bennett made his name in the revue Beyond the Fringe before writing plays.

clue.text: So to do is found to suit Agamemnon's daughter

definitions.text: So to do is found to suit Agamemnon's daughter

parts.words: So to do is found to suit Agamemnon's daughter
parts.note: Eugene O'Neill's trilogy title says grieving 'becomes' Electra; to do so is to grieve

explanation.surface: Some action is found fitting for Agamemnon's daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Becomes' in O'Neill's title Mourning Becomes Electra means 'suits'; the clue rewrites the title, asking for the verb whose -ing form suits Electra.
explanation.definitionFit: To grieve is what O'Neill's title says suits Electra, Agamemnon's daughter.

clue.text: Poet Alice, or my Ellen, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters of my Ellen could be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: A poet named Alice, or maybe a woman called Ellen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges MY ELLEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Alice Meynell was a Victorian and Edwardian Catholic poet and essayist.

clue.text: Piers Paul Read's parvenu

parts.note: a newly rich social climber, and the title of a 1973 novel by Piers Paul Read

explanation.walkthrough: Piers Paul Read's 1973 novel The Upstart follows a social climber; the clue uses the title's everyday sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A parvenu is a social climber newly risen to wealth, the sense of Read's novel title.

clue.text: Gunners discover Roman art on way back

parts.note: ars is the Latin word for art

indicators.note: on way back says the word for way is written in reverse

parts.note: a lane is a way or road

explanation.surface: Artillerymen uncover Roman art on the road home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns LANE into ENAL after ARS. The Gunners is the nickname of Arsenal football club, and also the arsenal's artillery.
explanation.definitionFit: Arsenal Football Club of London is nicknamed the Gunners, from its origins at the Woolwich armaments works.

clue.text: Greene's effective winner

parts.note: Graham Greene's novella title says one who fails takes everything, so in effect that person wins

explanation.walkthrough: Greene's Loser Takes All makes the one who loses the real winner, hence 'effective winner'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Graham Greene's Loser Takes All, the one who fails ends up taking everything.

clue.text: Bloom as part of July's sessions

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A flower blooms during summer sittings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloom' looks like a flower or blossoming; it is Leopold Bloom, hero of Joyce's novel, which is set on one June day.
explanation.definitionFit: Leopold Bloom is the central figure of James Joyce's novel, so the novel stands for its hero.

clue.text: Men sold ruined tombs

indicators.note: ruined signals the letters of men sold are wrecked and rebuilt

explanation.surface: Men sell off crumbling burial places.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' rearranges MEN SOLD.
explanation.definitionFit: Prehistoric stone burial chambers of upright slabs topped by a capstone are megalithic tombs.

clue.text: Unable to read when starting off sick (say again?)

indicators.note: starting off says the word for sick is removed from the front of the longer word

parts.note: one unable to read is illiterate
ill means sick

explanation.surface: Someone who cannot read, ill from the start, asks you to repeat yourself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starting off' takes ILL from the start of ILLITERATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To repeat or restate something is the verb sense of the definition's request.

clue.text: Isherwood's chattering girl?

parts.note: Christopher Isherwood's novella title combines a word for a chatterer with a girl's name

explanation.walkthrough: The title of Isherwood's 1945 novella about filmmaking reads as a prattler plus a girl's name, Violet; the Prater is in fact a Vienna park.
explanation.definitionFit: Christopher Isherwood's 1945 novella about a Viennese film director bears this title.
